Three examples follow the Apeere heading at 1149: Bi mo ba lowo, maa kole; Kaka ki n jale, maa seru; and Bi bolu ba ro be yoo jeko. The first and third are garbled (kole, yoo jeko), and no analysis is given (YORUBA-T2-W03-SOURCE-DEFECTS).

coverage.objective: Gbolohun akiyesi alatenumo: definition, the focus particle ni and three focus examples

evidence.explanation: The type is defined as the sentence that draws attention to one part of the whole sentence, with ni as its focus particle; focus may fall on the subject (oluwa), the object (abo) or the verb (oro-ise). The line uses curly quotes around Ni and spaces before commas and the full stop.

The base sentence Mo ra iwe at 1163 is followed by focus on the object (Iwe ni mo ra at 1165), on the verb (Rira ni mo iwe at 1167) and on the subject (Emi ni mo ra iwe at 1169). Line 1167 omits ra and so is not a well-formed focus construction; the three examples are unnumbered.

coverage.objective: Gbolohun iyisodi: definition and six examples

evidence.explanation: The type is defined as the sentence used to deny an event (ko isele). The definition is one line and gives no rule for forming the negative.

Six examples follow the Apeere heading at 1175: Bolu ko jeun and Baba ko yo (negative statements), then the pairs Se o maa lo? / N ko lo. and Bolu ti de? / Ko tii de. The last four are question-answer pairs rather than transformed negative sentences, so they do not illustrate the definition consistently (YORUBA-T2-W03-SOURCE-DEFECTS).

evidence.explanation: Line 1205 defines ila kiko as a traditional and lineage craft and says men, women and children all marked themselves in the old days; 1207 says the oloola made the marks, that it was men work, lists the tools abe sekele, osun, ose dudu and omi ogbin ewe feru, and gives the time as early morning (aaro kutukutu). Line 1249 repeats that the oloola made the marks but gives a different tool list (abe, omi igbin, abbl), so the two tool lists conflict and neither is complete.

coverage.objective: Importance and uses of ila, and where the marks were made on the body

evidence.explanation: Line 1209 heads AKOON (for AKOONU) and 1211 gives the sub-heading Pataki ati iwulo ila.

Facial marking is called one of the ways of adorning the body in the old days. The Yoruba marked in various patterns: on the cheek, the forehead and the jaw, and on the body from the chest down to the lower abdomen and from the back to the buttocks. The paragraph is one sentence split across three lines with missing spaces.

coverage.objective: Reasons for facial marks, the seven named patterns and the three definitions

evidence.explanation: Line 1221 says the reasons for facial marks are divided into ona m, but only two follow: identification (1223) and beauty (1225). The count word is truncated and does not match the two reasons given.
Line 1227 says the patterns vary from one region to another and lists seven: Pele, Baamu, Abaja, Keke, Ture, Gombo and Ila ondo. The list is unnumbered and not attributed to regions.

Only three patterns are defined: Pele as three vertical lines on the cheek among the Ijebu (1243), Gombo as a long line drawn from the head and lying across, among the Oyo, Ogbomoso, Iwo, Ede and Osogbo (1245), and Ila ondo as a single line on the cheek among the Ondo (1247). Baamu, Abaja, Keke and Ture are named but never described.

coverage.objective: Igbeyawo: meaning and value, the two families and the purpose of marriage

evidence.explanation: Line 1337 says marriage was never taken lightly in the old Yoruba society, that it was counted a serious matter and that everything connected with it was important. Line 1339 says the elements once counted important are no longer so today, gives marriage as a relationship between two families, then defines it at 1341 as the union of a man and a woman living together as husband and wife. Both paragraphs are run-on with missing spaces and garbled clauses (owo yepere, ko je ki igbeyawo pe mo) (YORUBA-T2-W04-SOURCE-DEFECTS).
Line 1343 says men take a wife to be a helper, and 1345 says the couple love each other so as to have aaro in life; aaro is unclear. Neither line is developed.

coverage.objective: The seven abinibi marriage steps listed in order

evidence.explanation: Line 1347 heads IGBESE IGBEYAWO and 1349 introduces the steps followed in the old days, duplicating igbese as igbese igbese. Seven steps follow, each marked with a leading hyphen rather than a number: Ifojusode (1351), Iwadii (1353), Alarina (1355), Isihun/ Ijohen (1357), Itoro (1359), Idana (1361) and Igbeyawo (1363). The list gives no summary of what each step is; that is supplied separately below.

coverage.objective: Ifojusode and Iwadii: the first two steps

evidence.explanation: Line 1369 defines ifojusode as the first step: when a young man matures he looks out for a woman he wants to marry, and in the old days the parents looked out for a wife for their son; beauty alone was not sought but also character. The label has no space after its hyphen, and the closing clause (bi ko se ati iwa) is garbled.

Line 1373 explains iwadii: the young man tells his parents, who investigate the girls mother because they believe a daughter takes after her mother. They look for diseases named as ete, warapa and ikofee, ask whether the family are ajigbese, and use the undefined abbreviation abbl. Line 1375 adds that they finally consult Ifa about how the marriage will go; the clause bi ifa ba fore abusebuse is garbled.

coverage.objective: Alarina: the intermediary and his investigation

evidence.explanation: Line 1377 calls alarina the third step and defines him as the iko who moves between the young man and the young woman who want each other; gbokegbodo and fe fe are garbled. Line 1379 says a key part of the work is a close investigation of the girl and her family, that the man who does it thoroughly is used as alarina because the work is delicate (ise elege), that he must know every trick to confirm the girl is hoo, and that the work ends once the two meet and see each other. It closes with the proverb bi oko ba moju aya tan alarena a yeba. The spelling alternates between alarina and alarena, and hoo, powe and moju are unclear (YORUBA-T2-W04-SOURCE-DEFECTS).

coverage.objective: Ijohen / Isihun: the acceptance and the fee

evidence.explanation: Line 1381 heads the step IJOHEN/ISIHUN, the reverse order of the list at 1357. Line 1383 says the girls family also investigates the young mans family for disease or debt, and that if no defect is found and the girl is willing she answers that she accepts; her acceptance is called ijohen or isihun. The same line fixes the fee at poun meji sile meji paid by the husband to his afesona, without saying whether that is a fixed custom or a local price. The paragraph has a duplicated fe, a missing space before Poun, and the undefined afesona.

coverage.objective: Itoro and Idana: the betrothal visit and the payment day

evidence.explanation: Line 1387 says that once the girl accepts, the young mans parents go to make itoro. The line says they go lodo awon obi omokunrin naa, repeating the boys parents where the girls parents are meant, and it has no full stop. It adds that the visit is where everyone knows the couple as afesona and the idana date is fixed.

Line 1391 defines the idana day as the day the young mans family pays in full everything the wifes family asks (patapata laiku eyokan), with a small feast; at that point the two are first known as husband and wife and the wedding day is fixed. Ariya ranpe lewaye and won to sese ma mo are garbled. No item of the payment is named, which is the gap recorded as YO-T2-W04-ASA-08.

coverage.objective: Igbeyawo: the wedding celebration and the third-night custom

evidence.explanation: Line 1395 says the scale of the wedding follows the wealth of the two families but that a noisy wedding (igbeyawo alariwo) must not be held; the clause gege bi iwadii ti won base is garbled. Line 1397 says the wife moves to her husbands house at irole, that before then she goes around receiving prayers and advice from her parents and family, and that on the third night the husband must approach her to learn whether she has known a man before. It states that a previous relationship is a disgrace for the wife and her family while chastity is good fortune for them. The paragraph is unmarked by any tone or sub-dot and several terms (owo irole, ero, gba a, n la) are unclear.

coverage.objective: Aayan ogbufo defined as the work of rendering one language in another

evidence.locator: heading, AKOONU and definition lines 1453, 1459 and 1461 (SHA-256 0fb18f89faf4250d469e62c1674d696a5894c8b243f035263da99a45451ededd; line 1461 f8a282e1b9cded98ace0126a36e0d7e5a2d534aad7cb1dd6c24954ece9a27b54)
evidence.explanation: Line 1453 heads ORI-ORO-;Aayan  Ogbufo with two spaces between Aayan and Ogbufo and the separator run into the title. Line 1459 heads AKOONU and line 1461 defines the term: Aayan ogbufo ni ise titumo ede kan si ede miiran, that is, translation is the work of rendering one language into another. The definition line has no full stop and gives no example; the example material comes only after the rules at 1491-1529.

coverage.objective: The translator must know the required English knowledge and understand Yoruba to its depth

evidence.explanation: Line 1465 states that before a translator can succeed at rendering meaning, the translator must know the tifun tedo of the English language and must also understand Yoruba down to its depth (tusu ede Yoruba naa de isale ikoko). tifun tedo is garbled and undefined, so what the translator must know of English is never stated. The line is a single sentence with a space before its comma; it gives no test, example or standard.

coverage.objective: Ilana sise aayan ogbufo: the six rules and cautions for translating

evidence.explanation: Three prohibitions: not every word in one language can be translated into another (1469, which writes ode miiran for ede miiran); do not translate sentence by sentence, because that spoils the beauty and the meaning of such a passage (1473); do not translate words individually, because that loses the meaning the translator wants to render (1477, which splits tu nu).

Three directives: reading and re-reading the passage is important before a translator can translate well (1481, where akoto to muna doko is garbled); the meaning labelled erefee is not adequate and it is the deep meaning that a translator needs (1485, where erefee is unclear); and the translator should use the names found in the passage (1489, which writes lo oruko). The six points are unnumbered and no worked example links any of them to the practice that follows, so the ilana is present as rules but not as a procedure (YORUBA-T2-W05-SOURCE-DEFECTS).

coverage.objective: Six English-Yoruba translation pairs used as classroom practice

evidence.explanation: Line 1491 says this is the translation exercise among the students in the class. Six English-Yoruba pairs follow with no numbers and no instruction. Pair 1 is Please bury the harchet against Jowo fiye denu (1495 and 1497, with harchet for hatchet and no full stop). Pair 2 is He who fight and run away, leaves to fight the other day against Agbo to feyinrin, agbara lo lo mu wa (1501 and 1503). Pair 3 is Time and tide wait for no man against Akoko ati igba ko duro de enikan (1507 and 1509).

Pair 4 is Paddle your own canoe against Gbo tire (1513 and 1515, which has a trailing tab). Pair 5 is They may have been drumming against Won ti le maa lu ilu (1519 and 1521, with a trailing space). Pair 6 is He came in reluctantly against O wole tikotiko (1525 and 1527). Line 1897 says that in the past pregnancy was not wished on a woman because of ese, that they de e so the pregnancy does not rise, that they use various oogun, that medicine is not usually given in the first to third month but after three months various medicines are used, including medicine to keep the child firm, to make the womb fuye, for ese and oogun abiwere. Line 1899 says some medicines are decoctions to drink, some to bathe in and some to lick, each with its own time, some in the third, fifth or seventh month. evidence.explanation: Line 1901 describes the woman kneeling and beginning gbin kikan-kikan when the pregnancy is advanced, with an elderly woman behind and another in front watching for the baby to show its head, and cloths spread to receive it. Line 1903 acknowledges that there may be difficulty and that they do what they know. Line 1905 heads OMO BIBI/ OJO IKUNLE; line 1909 names Ori ikunle as the woman who delivers, describes the blood and water that show the time has come, the instruction to gbin leralera, the two elderly women, and the agbebi who does what she can when there is difficulty. The heading is unpunctuated, gbin kikan-kikan and Ori ikunle are undefined, and 1901 runs into 1903 mid-sentence.

coverage.objective: Eewo ati oro idile: the family food prohibitions after childbirth

evidence.explanation: Line 1911 defines Oro ile as what a woman who has delivered must not do for her own benefit and for the child, and says oro idile differs from family to family. Line 1913 gives four family examples: idile olu oje, where she may not eat iyan or amala until the day of ikomojade and eats only isu and ekuru; idile onigbeeti, where the mother may not eat soup with salt or pepper until ikomojade, called obe ate; idile olokun esin, where pounded yam and beans with red palm oil are eaten until ikomo; and idile olofa, where obe ate and obe afun are eaten and the new mother eats oka amala igbako kan soso lemeeta lojumo. The family names, igbako, lemeeta and lojumo are unclear, the scheme says oro idile while the body says Oro ile, and neither eewo nor oro is defined.

coverage.objective: Igbagbo nipa abiku: the belief and the naming practice

evidence.explanation: Line 1915 heads IGBAGBO AWON YORUBA NIPA ABIKU and 1919 explains that abiku are children born repeatedly who die, that the Yoruba believe they belong to an egbe in heaven, that parents cut marks on the feet or hands of such a child while it sleeps, and that the belief says such a child will no longer leave its parents when it returns to the world, so the loss is called Abuku because the egbe will no longer receive it. It lists Kokumo, Fidimaye, Malomo, Kukoyi, Maku, Kosoko, Rotimi, Durosinmi and Kosoko again as names that show abiku. The belief is stated without qualification, Inu le bi and ge ika ese are garbled, the name list repeats Kosoko and the paragraph has no full stop at the heading.

coverage.objective: Scheme Week 7 LITIRESO objectives: itan oloro geere as a source of Yoruba history and culture; how the Yoruba bury the dead at home

evidence.explanation: Line 91 names itan oloro geere as a source of Yoruba history and culture and Asa bi Yoruba se n sin oku sinu ile, with a hyphen after Litireso, a semicolon between the two objectives and trailing spaces and tabs. The body heads LITIRESO at 1927 and repeats both objectives in a fused heading at 1929, then defines Litireso atenudenu at 1931, argues at 1933 that ewi atenudenu are the source of many itan and asa, and tells the Orunmila and Idi story at 1935-1961 to explain why the dead are buried. It never defines itan oloro geere as such and in the body oloro occurs only in the 1929 heading, so the objective is PARTIAL.

coverage.objective: Litireso atenudenu: the inherited oral ewi and itan as a source of history and culture

evidence.explanation: Line 1927 heads LITIRESO. Line 1929 fuses two headings, ITAN OLORO GEEREGEGE BI ORISUN ITAN ATI ASA YORUBA and ASA BI YORUBA SE N SIN OKU SI INU ILE, with semicolons between them. Line 1931 defines Litireso atenudenu as the ewi and itan inherited from the great-grandparents, oral because they could neither read nor write. Line 1933 says these ewi atenudenu are the source of many itan and much Yoruba asa, and that their itan atenudenu speak of isedale and the origin of culture, drawn from odu ifa, from the various wars of the past and from itan aroso adayeba. The heading writes GEEREGEGE where the scheme writes geere; 1931 fuses atenudenu-; and writes pea and mo-on-ko; 1933 writes orison, aria won and abajo, and leaves ogunto unclear.

coverage.objective: Asa bi Yoruba se n sin oku: the Orunmila and Idi story and the two reasons given for burial

evidence.explanation: Line 1935 announces the question of why the Yoruba bury the dead. Line 1937 says that in the past not every corpse was buried: a body was taken into the forest if the town was near, or thrown into the forest or into a hollow tree. Lines 1939-1959 tell the story of Orunmila and his wife Idi: their quarrel, Idi feigning death to escape with a lover, the bearers taking her body to the forest, the lover carrying her to Ejigbo, the market encounter and the song Bo o kola, kola / Bo o gbeni, o gbeni / Ewo laboro woju oloja, loja Ejigbo / A i i wo o / Oju oku lo n wo, and the discovery by Orunmila. Line 1959 concludes that from then on people bury a corpse instead of throwing it into the forest; 1961 gives the second reason, that no one sees a corpse face to face. Only these two reasons are given, no burial rite is described, and the story is heavily garbled (Kop e ko jinna, Were ,Idi, bag be, togbe, tubo n ww o).

coverage.objective: Igbelewon (1971-1975) and Ise asetilewa (1977-1997): two questions and five multiple-choice questions on onka

evidence.explanation: IGBELEWON at 1971 asks Ona meloo ni onka Yoruba pin si (1973) and then Kin ni a fi n da okookan mo. Salaye re pelu apeere (1975), numbered 1 then b, with no final punctuation and no answer.

Five questions follow ISE ASETILEWA at 1977. Q1 (1979) asks which sound marks most onkaye, with options n, m and t; Q2 (1983) asks which sound marks onkapo, with options I, m and n; Q3 (1987) asks what Orinlenirinwo is, with options 440, 480 and 490; Q4 (1991) asks what Egbaa is, with options 2000, 200 and 20,000; Q5 (1997) asks what 14,000 is, with options togoje, egbaaje and irinwo. Every list is (a), (b), (d) with c omitted, the blanks in Q1 and Q2 differ in length, Q5 puts its options on the question line, no key is given and the capitalisation of the options is inconsistent.

coverage.objective: Igbelewon (1921-1923) and Apa keji 2 (2005-2007): questions on itoju oyun, lekun-un-rere and the burial of the dead

evidence.explanation: IGBELEWON at 1921 sets one question, Salaye orisii ona ti awon Yoruba n gba se itoju oyun ni aye atijo, dated to the past, with a trailing tab and no answer. It covers the itoju oyun objective only.

Apa keji Q2 at 2005 repeats the Igbelewon question almost word for word: Daruko orisii ona ti awon Yoruba n gba lati se itoju oyun laye atijo. Line 2007 labels its second part b and asks salaye lekun-un-rere, idi ti awon Yoruba fi n sin oku, mixing an unclear term with the literature objective; the numbering runs 2 then b and no answer is given.

coverage.objective: Apa keji 1 (2001-2003): the two divisions of onka and how each is marked

evidence.explanation: APA KEJI at 1999 heads a mixed block. Q1 at 2001 asks Ona meloo ni onka Yoruba pin si? and 2003 labels its second part b, Kin ni a fi n da won mo. Q1 repeats the EDE Igbelewon at 1973 word for word and b repeats 1975 without Salaye re pelu apeere, is numbered 1 then b, gives no answer or marking, and the block then moves to ASA at 2005 and LIT at 2007 without a strand label.
